course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 5
unit.description: Follow Manifest Destiny and the Mexican–American War, the sectional conflict over slavery, the election of 1860 and secession, the Civil War, and Reconstruction and its failure from 1844 to 1877.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: Sectional Conflict: Regional Differences
lesson.summary: How immigration and nativism changed the North, how free labor and slave labor divided the economies of the two sections, and how abolitionists and defenders of slavery argued over slavery.
learningGoals: Explain the effects of immigration from Europe and Asia on American culture from 1844 to 1877.
Explain how the free-labor North and the slave-labor South developed opposed views of western expansion.
Explain the arguments of free-soilers, abolitionists, and defenders of slavery.
lesson.bigIdea: Immigration changed Northern society, and the North's free-labor economy and the South's slave-labor economy produced opposed responses to the spread of slavery.
lesson.context: This topic covers two learning objectives: the effects of immigration on American culture and the regional differences over slavery that caused tension before the Civil War. The CED asks you to read sources for their purpose and point of view, so note who is speaking and to whom.

sections.title: Immigration and nativism

blocks.text: Substantial numbers of international migrants continued to arrive in the United States from Europe and Asia, mainly from Ireland and Germany, often settling in ethnic communities where they could preserve elements of their languages and customs. Many Irish migrants fled the famine that began in 1845 and settled in Northern cities, where they worked on canals and railroads and in factories. Many Germans, some of them fleeing the failed revolutions of 1848, settled as farmers in the Midwest and in cities such as Milwaukee and St. Louis. Chinese migrants came to California, many of them to work in the mines. The newcomers built churches, newspapers, and schools, and they increased the number of Roman Catholics in the United States, which changed American religious and cultural life.

A strongly anti-Catholic nativist movement arose that was aimed at limiting new immigrants' political power and cultural influence. Nativist mobs attacked Catholic churches and homes in Philadelphia in 1844. In the 1850s the American Party, whose members were called the Know-Nothings, won elections in several states by calling for longer waiting periods before immigrants could become citizens and vote. The party broke apart over slavery.

sections.takeaway: Irish and German immigration reshaped Northern society, and nativists tried to limit the political power of the newcomers.

sections.title: Free labor and the free-soil movement
sections.conceptTitle: Free labor and the free-soil movement

blocks.text: The North's expanding manufacturing economy relied on free labor, in contrast to the Southern economy's dependence on enslaved labor. By 1860 nearly four million people were enslaved in the South, and cotton, grown by their labor, was the nation's leading export. Some Northerners did not object to slavery on principle but claimed that slavery would undermine the free labor market. As a result, a free-soil movement arose that portrayed the expansion of slavery as incompatible with free labor.

Free-soilers believed that a worker should be able to rise through his own effort and feared that slaveholders would take the best western land and leave no room for free farmers and wage earners. Many free-soilers held racial prejudices, and some wanted the territories kept for white settlers. The Free-Soil Party of 1848 and, later, the Republican Party of the 1850s gave the movement a political voice.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Free-soilers and abolitionists were not the same. Abolitionists wanted to end slavery everywhere, while many free-soilers wanted only to stop its spread in order to protect free labor.

sections.takeaway: The free-labor North feared that slavery would crowd out free workers in the West, and the free-soil movement grew from that fear.

sections.title: Abolitionists and defenders of slavery

blocks.text: African American and white abolitionists, although a minority in the North, mounted a highly visible campaign against slavery, presenting moral arguments against the institution, assisting escapes, and sometimes expressing a willingness to use violence to achieve their goals. William Lloyd Garrison's newspaper The Liberator demanded immediate emancipation, and Frederick Douglass began to publish The North Star in 1847. Harriet Tubman and many others helped enslaved people to escape on the Underground Railroad. John Brown, who believed that violence was justified, led a raid on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, in 1859.

Defenders of slavery based their arguments on racial doctrines, the view that slavery was a positive social good, and the belief that slavery and states' rights were protected by the Constitution. John C. Calhoun and writers such as George Fitzhugh claimed that slavery benefited enslaved people and society, and they relied on false claims about the inferiority of Black people. The House of Representatives adopted a “gag rule” from 1836 to 1844 that set aside antislavery petitions without reading them, and Southern states restricted the circulation of antislavery writings.

sections.takeaway: Abolitionists attacked slavery on moral grounds, and its defenders answered with racial doctrines, claims of social benefit, and appeals to the Constitution.

connections.title: From argument to political crisis
connections.body: The opposed views of free-soilers, abolitionists, and defenders of slavery shaped the political events of the 1850s. Topic 5.6 follows them.
connections.transferQuestion: How did the arguments of defenders of slavery in the 1850s differ from the views of Southern leaders in the early republic?
connections.feedback: A strong answer notes that many early leaders called slavery a necessary evil, while by the 1830s and 1850s defenders called it a positive good and relied on racial doctrines.
